### Reviewer 1

In the present manuscript the authors test the idea that IRE1α alters the vascular network of islets to impeach their function through intersecting antiangiogenic TSP1. The hypothesis is tested using a range of approaches foremost being mutant mice that lack IRE1α in vascular endothelial cells uniformly and pathway suppression with siRNA methods. Young mice lacking IRE1α were fed a diet high in fat and metabolic readouts characterized. The text is further supported by helpful supplemental figures with control data. Overall, the composition is clear and easy to follow. A few minor usage issues were encountered but not enough to detract from the reading of the text. The data support the conclusions mostly, although certain aspects lack signaling direction and specificity and these points are explained in detail below.
Strategic/novelty: The hypothesis is new, as are the findings. However, a link between IRE1α and TSP1 was noted (J Cell Mol Med. 2022 Oct;26(20):5303-5314). Further, links between human islets and TSP1 and the dominant TSP1 receptor CD47 was published (Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab. 2023 Apr 1;324(4): E347-E357). Also, a link between TSP1-CD47 and glucose homeostasis was made in mice on a HFD (Cells. 2020 Jul 15;9(7):1695). These points are emphasized not to lessen the present work. Still these references should be covered in the Introduction and/or Discussion section of the manuscript to give a balanced presentation of the existing literature in relation to the new findings.
Balance in presentation: Not to belabor the ideas noted above, but here is an example of limited and erroneous use of citations by the authors. They cite the following 2 papers when introducing their data on TSP1 – (1) Molecular basis for the regulation of angiogenesis by thrombospondin-1 and -2. Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med 2, a006627 (2012) from Jack Lawler at Harvard. The issue here is the year of publication 2012 so it misses many more recent findings. The second citation, Thrombospondin 1 in Metabolic Diseases. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne) 12, 638536 (2021), was from folks in Pennsylvania that have done only a little work in this area. More importantly, one should always cite primary papers and in this case some that show how TSP1 limits ECs, vascular pathways, blood flow, self-renewal (see effects on cMyc), and metabolism. See Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005 Sep 13;102(37):13141-6 and others by this same group.
Methods: Please provide detailed information on animal usage: ACUC protocol #, anesthesia and euthanasia methods, balancing and mitigation of the cage effect, randomization of animals into treatment groups (was a software program used for this and if yes please state). Explain how cohort size was arrived at. Please provide details on the methods used to blind the researchers to treatment groups, etc. Justify using young mice and if only one sex was used justify why both were not studied.
Data: Counting CD31+ cells is a common metric employed to characterize vascularization. Yet, it gives no information concerning real-time tissue perfusion. This is a valid point as TSP1 seems to limit perfusion of various vascular beds separate from inhibiting cell and specifically EC proliferation and migration. Some analysis of organ (i.e., pancreas) and organoid (i.e., islet) blood flow should be made in the mice from the various treatment groups.
The paper is light on details on the signaling mechanism(s) at play. We do not the source of the TSP1 in the islets that is putatively the cause of issues and a target for IRE1α. A change in mRNA suggests a cell type may be the source but not more. The literature finds many stressed cell types from many species and people make TSP1. However, some data already pointed out in mice lacking the TSP1 signal versus circulating cell lacking TSP1 found the effect resided in the parenchyma and not in the circulating cells.
We do not know the receptors that secreated TSP1 acts through in the islets to negatively impact glucose homeostasis. One place to begin would be to look at WT and IRE1α null EC receptor patterns for primary TSP1 receptors such as CD36, CD47, beta integrins, and SIRPα. TSP1 apparently has several domains that can bind to one of these receptors and adversely alter redox pathways and metabolism. After the authors define the cell surface landscape, they should treat cells with TSP1 ± TSP1 receptor blockers and then characterize proliferation, cell death, etc.
The authors might also consider testing possible direct effects of IRE1α on vascular nitric oxide. See Mol Cells. 2018 Nov 30;41(11):964-970 and Aging (Albany NY). 2023 Dec 13;15(23):13608-13627.
Why was there had only a partial loss in IRE1α protein in the lung EC of the mutant mice. All westerns need molecular marker dye lane. I find just placing the expected MW adjacent to a blot leaves out key information that as the reader I wish to consider for myself. Included the original full blots too.
Many blots of TSP1 find it at about 150 kD. The blot in Fig. 5F has it assigned a MW of 170. Please comment on this. BTW, TSP1 is up in the plasma of people with T1 and T2 diabetes. The Discussion section should point this out and cite the several papers that showed this.
This being the case, I am wondering if more detail in plasma TSP1 analysis can be given. Care is needed to not activate platelets as they were found decades ago to hold lots of pre-made TSP1. And the lack of impact of HF diet on plasma TSP1 is curious. Would a longer disease timeline alter this?
The TSP1 translation blocking morpholino gave only a partial suppression. Was a dose and time interval study done to optimize the conditions?
Additional information: A table summarizing all antibodies, manufacture details, dilutions, and validation of specificity information should be included.
Figures: These were nicely done, and one can get the point fast. And the legends were well done with n numbers and stat test used included for each.

### Reviewer 2

The main finding of this manuscript is that genetic depletion of IRE1 alpha in endothelial cells leads to glucose intolerance, blunted intra-islet angiogenesis, compensatory islet growth and enhanced endothelial cells thbs1 expression in high-fat diet-fed mice. Further, the author report that genetic deletion of thbs1 in endothelial cells corrected the defects in glucose homeostasis observed in HFD-fed mice with genetic deletion of IRE1alpha in endothelial cells. The authors conclude that their findings “uncover a critical role of the endothelial IRE1alpha suppression of THBS1 in governing the vascular support that enables the functional adaptation of islets during metabolic stress”. However, substantial issues have been identified that limit the interpretation of the data.
Comments:
- The genetic mouse models need further validation, including confirmation that gene expression and protein levels of IRE1alpha and THBS1 are significantly reduced in other tissues than lung, especially in islets and in tissues involved in glucose homeostasis, but also confirmation that their levels are not altered in other cell types than endothelial cells.
- For the in vivo studies, the authors must show data from VE-cadherin-Cre-ERT2 mice without tamoxifen injection to confirm that data are not related to the CRE expression only.
- Based on the data shown on both Figure 1 and figure 8, the authors cannot conclude that there is glucose intolerance and deficient insulin production. Indeed, the authors report insulin data without taking in account and correcting for glucose data at the same time. The authors can absolutely not conclude that fasting insulin and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion are decreased without reporting the glucose data, since insulin is dependent on glucose levels. Further, on both figure 1 and figure 8, glucose tolerance must be calculated as iAUC during the OGTT.
- The authors must report data in female and/or at least justify why they did only report data in male mice
- Information about the methods and experiments is lacking throughout the manuscript. For example, there is no information regarding how blood was drawn for insulin measurement (Fig 1) or how islets were processed for insulin content measurement (Fig 2). For histo and immunohistochemistry, the authors must have used IgG isotype as negative controls for staining. The n are very low for several experiments; only representative images of one experiment are shown (e.g. Fig 1b, Fig S1,..) and some figures show only replicate of one experiment (e.g. GSIS and perifusion data on Fig3).
- Beta-cell and alpha cell area and mass rather than % of alpha and beta-cell must be correctly calculated and reported to allow the authors to conclude there are changes in islet morphology.

### Reviewer 3

In this report, the authors demonstrate that genetic deletion of the inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1α) specifically in the endothelial cells of the adult mice, results in the poor response of the vascular cells to the metabolic stress induced by enforced obesity secondary to chronic high fat diet (HFD) intake. These abnormalities in IRE1α deficient endothelial cells were manifested in subtle glucose intolerance with impaired insulin secretion. The mechanism of this metabolic dysregulation was mediated through upregulation of the mRNA encoding presumed anti-angiogenic agent thrombospondin-1 (THBS1/TSP1). IRE1α RNase15 mediated mRNA decay of THBS1 presumably modulate the overall expression of this factor in SV40 large T antigen immortalized MS1 mouse endothelial cells. Knock down of THBS1 in endothelial cells restored the islet vascular defects arising from endothelial cell-IRE1α deficiency in response to HDF induced obesity.
Comments:
The mechanism by which neo-angiogenesis might play a role in the regulation of obesity induced metabolic dysfunction is not known. Demonstration that IRE1α deficiency through upregulation of THBS1 might interfere with angiogenic activity in the islets thereby contributing to metabolic derangements afforded by chronic HDF induced obesity could have therapeutic implications.
However, the data presented are not that convincing and many of the conclusions are not strongly supported by the data provided.
1) The majority of the changes in glucose levels and insulin intolerance in the IRE1α deficient mice are only marginal, which are corrected with the THBS1 knock down. Indeed, the pathophysiological consequences of those metabolic changes are not readily apparent. Are there any pathological changes in the cardiovascular function, liver metabolism or kidney function in the IRE1α deficient mice ?
2) It is unclear whether the subtle differences in hyperglycemia and insulin intolerance are primarily due to pancreatic dysfunction or increase in the adipose tissue vascular mass changes secondary to the chronic HFD induced obesity? Is there a correlation with the increase vascular mass index with the metabolic changes potentially in the adipose tissue of the IRE1α or THBS1 deficient mice.
3) The authors claim that there could be a defect in the islet angiogenesis in the IRE1α or THBS1 deficient mice. However, whether there are changes in the vessel density and as to how these changes lead to metabolic abnormalities observed is not well characterized. In figure 4 the authors use CD31 (PECAM) as the marker for endothelial cell staining. However, CD31 staining is not sufficient to specifically stain endothelial cells as CD31 is also expressed on hematopoietic cells including inflammatory monocytes and macrophages. Other vascular specific markers such as VE-cadherin or CD34 might be considered.
4) The use of mouse MS1 SV40 large T antigen immortalized endothelial cells could be fraught with artifacts because metabolically these cells employ oxidative phosphorylation, but not glycolysis, secondary to oncogenic transformation possibly obscuring the effects I IRE1α and XBP1 mediated stress responses. Use of more primary isolated endothelial cells, preferably from the metabolic organs might be more revealing.
5) In IRE1α deficient mice there are also changes in the expression and RNA decay of other factors. Then, is THBS1 dysregulation the main factor that contributes to the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction in the IRE1α mice? Why the authors elected to focus on THBS1 and not the other factors.
6) THBS1 has many different pleiotropic effects on regulating blood vessel integrity. Besides potential anti-angiogenic effect, THSP1 could also modulate homeostatic functions of blood vessels not only in the pancreas but also in adipose or liver vasculature. Then, to what extent the metabolic changes in IRE1α or THSP1 deficient mice, could be attributed to its anti-angiogenic activity?

### Reviewer 1

In the present manuscript the authors test the idea that IRE1α alters the vascular network of islets to impeach their function through intersecting antiangiogenic TSP1. The hypothesis is tested using a range of approaches foremost being mutant mice that lack IRE1α in vascular endothelial cells uniformly and pathway suppression with siRNA methods. Young mice lacking IRE1α were fed a diet high in fat and metabolic readouts characterized. The text is further supported by helpful supplemental figures with control data. Overall, the composition is clear and easy to follow. A few minor usage issues were encountered but not enough to detract from the reading of the text. The data support the conclusions mostly, although certain aspects lack signaling direction and specificity and these points are explained in detail below.
Strategic/novelty: The hypothesis is new, as are the findings. However, a link between IRE1α and TSP1 was noted (J Cell Mol Med. 2022 Oct;26(20):5303-5314). Further, links between human islets and TSP1 and the dominant TSP1 receptor CD47 was published (Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab. 2023 Apr 1;324(4): E347-E357). Also, a link between TSP1-CD47 and glucose homeostasis was made in mice on a HFD (Cells. 2020 Jul 15;9(7):1695). These points are emphasized not to lessen the present work. Still these references should be covered in the Introduction and/or Discussion section of the manuscript to give a balanced presentation of the existing literature in relation to the new findings.
Balance in presentation: Not to belabor the ideas noted above, but here is an example of limited and erroneous use of citations by the authors. They cite the following 2 papers when introducing their data on TSP1 – (1) Molecular basis for the regulation of angiogenesis by thrombospondin-1 and -2. Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med 2, a006627 (2012) from Jack Lawler at Harvard. The issue here is the year of publication 2012 so it misses many more recent findings. The second citation, Thrombospondin 1 in Metabolic Diseases. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne) 12, 638536 (2021), was from folks in Pennsylvania that have done only a little work in this area. More importantly, one should always cite primary papers and in this case some that show how TSP1 limits ECs, vascular pathways, blood flow, self-renewal (see effects on cMyc), and metabolism. See Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005 Sep 13;102(37):13141-6 and others by this same group.
Methods: Please provide detailed information on animal usage: ACUC protocol #, anesthesia and euthanasia methods, balancing and mitigation of the cage effect, randomization of animals into treatment groups (was a software program used for this and if yes please state). Explain how cohort size was arrived at. Please provide details on the methods used to blind the researchers to treatment groups, etc. Justify using young mice and if only one sex was used justify why both were not studied.
Data: Counting CD31+ cells is a common metric employed to characterize vascularization. Yet, it gives no information concerning real-time tissue perfusion. This is a valid point as TSP1 seems to limit perfusion of various vascular beds separate from inhibiting cell and specifically EC proliferation and migration. Some analysis of organ (i.e., pancreas) and organoid (i.e., islet) blood flow should be made in the mice from the various treatment groups.
The paper is light on details on the signaling mechanism(s) at play. We do not the source of the TSP1 in the islets that is putatively the cause of issues and a target for IRE1α. A change in mRNA suggests a cell type may be the source but not more. The literature finds many stressed cell types from many species and people make TSP1. However, some data already pointed out in mice lacking the TSP1 signal versus circulating cell lacking TSP1 found the effect resided in the parenchyma and not in the circulating cells.
We do not know the receptors that secreated TSP1 acts through in the islets to negatively impact glucose homeostasis. One place to begin would be to look at WT and IRE1α null EC receptor patterns for primary TSP1 receptors such as CD36, CD47, beta integrins, and SIRPα. TSP1 apparently has several domains that can bind to one of these receptors and adversely alter redox pathways and metabolism. After the authors define the cell surface landscape, they should treat cells with TSP1 ± TSP1 receptor blockers and then characterize proliferation, cell death, etc.
The authors might also consider testing possible direct effects of IRE1α on vascular nitric oxide. See Mol Cells. 2018 Nov 30;41(11):964-970 and Aging (Albany NY). 2023 Dec 13;15(23):13608-13627.
Why was there had only a partial loss in IRE1α protein in the lung EC of the mutant mice. All westerns need molecular marker dye lane. I find just placing the expected MW adjacent to a blot leaves out key information that as the reader I wish to consider for myself. Included the original full blots too.
Many blots of TSP1 find it at about 150 kD. The blot in Fig. 5F has it assigned a MW of 170. Please comment on this. BTW, TSP1 is up in the plasma of people with T1 and T2 diabetes. The Discussion section should point this out and cite the several papers that showed this.
This being the case, I am wondering if more detail in plasma TSP1 analysis can be given. Care is needed to not activate platelets as they were found decades ago to hold lots of pre-made TSP1. And the lack of impact of HF diet on plasma TSP1 is curious. Would a longer disease timeline alter this?
The TSP1 translation blocking morpholino gave only a partial suppression. Was a dose and time interval study done to optimize the conditions?
Additional information: A table summarizing all antibodies, manufacture details, dilutions, and validation of specificity information should be included.
Figures: These were nicely done, and one can get the point fast. And the legends were well done with n numbers and stat test used included for each.

### Reviewer 2

The main finding of this manuscript is that genetic depletion of IRE1 alpha in endothelial cells leads to glucose intolerance, blunted intra-islet angiogenesis, compensatory islet growth and enhanced endothelial cells thbs1 expression in high-fat diet-fed mice. Further, the author report that genetic deletion of thbs1 in endothelial cells corrected the defects in glucose homeostasis observed in HFD-fed mice with genetic deletion of IRE1alpha in endothelial cells. The authors conclude that their findings “uncover a critical role of the endothelial IRE1alpha suppression of THBS1 in governing the vascular support that enables the functional adaptation of islets during metabolic stress”. However, substantial issues have been identified that limit the interpretation of the data.
Comments:
- The genetic mouse models need further validation, including confirmation that gene expression and protein levels of IRE1alpha and THBS1 are significantly reduced in other tissues than lung, especially in islets and in tissues involved in glucose homeostasis, but also confirmation that their levels are not altered in other cell types than endothelial cells.
- For the in vivo studies, the authors must show data from VE-cadherin-Cre-ERT2 mice without tamoxifen injection to confirm that data are not related to the CRE expression only.
- Based on the data shown on both Figure 1 and figure 8, the authors cannot conclude that there is glucose intolerance and deficient insulin production. Indeed, the authors report insulin data without taking in account and correcting for glucose data at the same time. The authors can absolutely not conclude that fasting insulin and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion are decreased without reporting the glucose data, since insulin is dependent on glucose levels. Further, on both figure 1 and figure 8, glucose tolerance must be calculated as iAUC during the OGTT.
- The authors must report data in female and/or at least justify why they did only report data in male mice
- Information about the methods and experiments is lacking throughout the manuscript. For example, there is no information regarding how blood was drawn for insulin measurement (Fig 1) or how islets were processed for insulin content measurement (Fig 2). For histo and immunohistochemistry, the authors must have used IgG isotype as negative controls for staining. The n are very low for several experiments; only representative images of one experiment are shown (e.g. Fig 1b, Fig S1,..) and some figures show only replicate of one experiment (e.g. GSIS and perifusion data on Fig3).
- Beta-cell and alpha cell area and mass rather than % of alpha and beta-cell must be correctly calculated and reported to allow the authors to conclude there are changes in islet morphology.

### Reviewer 3

In this report, the authors demonstrate that genetic deletion of the inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1α) specifically in the endothelial cells of the adult mice, results in the poor response of the vascular cells to the metabolic stress induced by enforced obesity secondary to chronic high fat diet (HFD) intake. These abnormalities in IRE1α deficient endothelial cells were manifested in subtle glucose intolerance with impaired insulin secretion. The mechanism of this metabolic dysregulation was mediated through upregulation of the mRNA encoding presumed anti-angiogenic agent thrombospondin-1 (THBS1/TSP1). IRE1α RNase15 mediated mRNA decay of THBS1 presumably modulate the overall expression of this factor in SV40 large T antigen immortalized MS1 mouse endothelial cells. Knock down of THBS1 in endothelial cells restored the islet vascular defects arising from endothelial cell-IRE1α deficiency in response to HDF induced obesity.
Comments:
The mechanism by which neo-angiogenesis might play a role in the regulation of obesity induced metabolic dysfunction is not known. Demonstration that IRE1α deficiency through upregulation of THBS1 might interfere with angiogenic activity in the islets thereby contributing to metabolic derangements afforded by chronic HDF induced obesity could have therapeutic implications.
However, the data presented are not that convincing and many of the conclusions are not strongly supported by the data provided.
1) The majority of the changes in glucose levels and insulin intolerance in the IRE1α deficient mice are only marginal, which are corrected with the THBS1 knock down. Indeed, the pathophysiological consequences of those metabolic changes are not readily apparent. Are there any pathological changes in the cardiovascular function, liver metabolism or kidney function in the IRE1α deficient mice ?
2) It is unclear whether the subtle differences in hyperglycemia and insulin intolerance are primarily due to pancreatic dysfunction or increase in the adipose tissue vascular mass changes secondary to the chronic HFD induced obesity? Is there a correlation with the increase vascular mass index with the metabolic changes potentially in the adipose tissue of the IRE1α or THBS1 deficient mice.
3) The authors claim that there could be a defect in the islet angiogenesis in the IRE1α or THBS1 deficient mice. However, whether there are changes in the vessel density and as to how these changes lead to metabolic abnormalities observed is not well characterized. In figure 4 the authors use CD31 (PECAM) as the marker for endothelial cell staining. However, CD31 staining is not sufficient to specifically stain endothelial cells as CD31 is also expressed on hematopoietic cells including inflammatory monocytes and macrophages. Other vascular specific markers such as VE-cadherin or CD34 might be considered.
4) The use of mouse MS1 SV40 large T antigen immortalized endothelial cells could be fraught with artifacts because metabolically these cells employ oxidative phosphorylation, but not glycolysis, secondary to oncogenic transformation possibly obscuring the effects I IRE1α and XBP1 mediated stress responses. Use of more primary isolated endothelial cells, preferably from the metabolic organs might be more revealing.
5) In IRE1α deficient mice there are also changes in the expression and RNA decay of other factors. Then, is THBS1 dysregulation the main factor that contributes to the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction in the IRE1α mice? Why the authors elected to focus on THBS1 and not the other factors.
6) THBS1 has many different pleiotropic effects on regulating blood vessel integrity. Besides potential anti-angiogenic effect, THSP1 could also modulate homeostatic functions of blood vessels not only in the pancreas but also in adipose or liver vasculature. Then, to what extent the metabolic changes in IRE1α or THSP1 deficient mice, could be attributed to its anti-angiogenic activity?

including the MW marker dye lane. We will provide all the original full blots in the

clearly. We included the iAUC for the GTT results in both Fig 1f and Fig 8c, which

HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO;Thbs1EC-KO mice relative to their control littermates. We also
included the data on serum glucose levels of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice after a 4-hour
fast when showing their serum insulin levels (Fig. 1h), which suggests the reduced
insulin levels did not result from lower glucose levels. For glucose-stimulated insulin
secretion in vivo, we observed marked reductions in insulin levels from HFD-fed
Ern1EC-KO mice (Fig. 1i) following glucose stimulation during the GTT (Fig. 1f),

Response:
We followed the suggestions from the Reviewer and performed dietary obesity analysis
for female Ern1EC-KO and Ern1fl/fl mice, which showed lower sensitivity to HFD-
induced obesity (data were presented in Supplemental Fig. S3 of the revised

Response:
We appreciate these important points from the Reviewer and included the information
about the methods and experiments in the Methods section, including how blood was
drawn for insulin measurement and how islets were processed for insulin content
measurement. For immunohistochemistry staining analysis of Insulin, CD31 and CD34
from pancreas sections, we used IgG as the negative control (Supplemental Fig. S6a).
For key metabolic phenotypes, we combined the n from repeated independent cohorts
for reaching a higher n number. Usually we presented representative images from at
least two independent experiments. We removed the flow-cytometry data in Fig 1b of
the previous manuscript as we employed a better method for isolating tissue ECs as
described in the Methods section. For islet perifusion data, we showed results from
pooled islets of HFD-fed mice (n=3 mice for each group, 2 independent animal cohorts).
For islet GSIS assay, we presented data from pooled islets in one animal cohort study
(Fig 3f), and similar data from another independent study, which is difficult to combine
when presenting the actual insulin valuse, is shown below for your information.
Primary islets of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice showed decreased glucose stimulated
insulin secretion.

Response:

primary islets from these models in Fig 4e.

Response:
We do agree with Reviewer in that endothelial IRE1α depletion did not lead to very
dramatic changes in glucose metabolism and insulin intolerance, but it did result in
impaired islet adaptation following HFD feeding. While we are very interested in
conducting more thorough studies such as the effects on their cardiovascular function,
liver metabolism and kidney function in this animal model, we did not observe apparent
pathological changes in their heart or kidney function. Surely enough, we will look into
opportunities for collaborating with colleagues in relevant fields to investigate these
important questions using appropriate stress conditions in the future. In the current
dietary obesity model, we conducted more experiments to examine lipid metabolism in
the liver, and we observed elevated levels of hepatic TAG and cholesterol in HFD-fed
Ern1EC-KO mice (data presented in Supplemental Fig. S1g and S1h), despite no apparent
histological changes in the liver via H/E staining analysis. Because this study focused
on glucose metabolism under obesity-induced metabolic stress, we would like to further
investigate in more mechanistic detail the role of endothelial IRE1α in hepatic lipid
metabolism following NASH-diet feeding or liver injuries. In this case, we will actively
seek more sufficient research funding support for these highly interesting studies in the
future.

mass changes secondary to the chronic HFD induced obesity? Is there a correlation with

Response:
This is a very insightful point that, in fact, led us to establish initially the DIO model,
as we anticipated a likely impact of endothelial IRE1α depletion upon adipose tissue
function in obesity. Unexpectedly but intriguingly, we found that the intra-islet ECs are
most sensitive to the loss of IRE1α during dietary obesity. We did not observe
significant alterations in the vascular density in adipose tissue of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO
mice (Supplemental Fig. S6e-g) or HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO;Thbs1EC-KO mice (Supplemental
Fig. S14b). This may reflect the distinct regulatory actions of endothelial IRE1α in
different tissues.
3) The authors claim that there could be a defect in the islet angiogenesis in the IRE1α
or THBS1 deficient mice. However, whether there are changes in the vessel density and
as to how these changes lead to metabolic abnormalities observed is not well
characterized. In figure 4 the authors use CD31 (PECAM) as the marker for endothelial
cell staining. However, CD31 staining is not sufficient to specifically stain endothelial
cells as CD31 is also expressed on hematopoietic cells including inflammatory
monocytes and macrophages. Other vascular specific markers such as VE-cadherin or
CD34 might be considered.
Response:
Following the Reviewer’s suggestions, we more carefully characterized the vascular
density in pancreatic islets, liver and adipose tissue of NC- and HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO
mice using CD31 as well as CD34 as the EC staining marker (Supplemental Fig. S6).
Consistently, we detected significantly reduced abundance of intra-islet ECs but not in
the liver or adipose tissue of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice, suggesting defective angiogenic
capacity in the islets under metabolic stress.
4) The use of mouse MS1 SV40 large T antigen immortalized endothelial cells could
be fraught with artifacts because metabolically these cells employ oxidative
phosphorylation, but not glycolysis, secondary to oncogenic transformation possibly
obscuring the effects I IRE1α and XBP1 mediated stress responses. Use of more
primary isolated endothelial cells, preferably from the metabolic organs might be more
revealing.
Response:
We appreciate this important point from the Reviewer. We followed the suggestions
and used primary HUVECs for dissecting the effect of IRE1α knockdown upon TSP1
expression (Supplemental Fig 6b, 6d and 6f). Notably, similar results were obtained as
in MS1 cells.
5) In IRE1α deficient mice there are also changes in the expression and RNA decay of
other factors. Then, is THBS1 dysregulation the main factor that contributes to the
pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction in the IRE1α mice? Why the authors elected to
focus on THBS1 and not the other factors.
Response:
We identified THBS1 as one of the top-ranked downregulated target genes as a result
of IRE1α ablation (Fig. 5). Moreover, based on the scRNA-seq analysis of HFD-fed
islets (accession No. GSE203376), we found that its expression is specifically restricted
to ECs along with the EC marker Cdh5 (Fig S10). Given TSP1 as a well-established
endogenous antiangiogenic factor that not only inhibits EC proliferation but also exerts
multiple regulatory effects upon glucose and lipid metabolism through affecting the
adipose tissue as well as pancreatic islets, we chose to focus on this molecule as a
potential downstream effector of IRE1α. Indeed, depletion of TSP1 in the context of
IRE1α ablation completely corrected the metabolic defects during dietary obesity (Fig
8), supporting that THBS1 dysregulation is the main factor contributing to the
metabolic dysfunction of islets in EC-specific IRE1α-deficient mice during dietary
obesity.
6) THBS1 has many different pleiotropic effects on regulating blood vessel integrity.
Besides potential anti-angiogenic effect, THSP1 could also modulate homeostatic
functions of blood vessels not only in the pancreas but also in adipose or liver
vasculature. Then, to what extent the metabolic changes in IRE1α or THSP1 deficient
mice, could be attributed to its anti-angiogenic activity?
Response:
We agree with the Reviewer in that IRE1α or TSP1 in ECs may exert additional
regulatory effects upon the endocrine cells in the islets, e.g. through intercellular
interactions that remain to be elucidated, in addition to their anti-angiogenic activity.
Nonetheless, our results together from the animal models and cell-based assays indicate
that the effect of TSP1’s anti-angiogenic activity in islets most likely serves as one
major contributor to the metabolic changes arising from endothelial IRE1α deficiency,
as we observed no overt changes in vascular density in the liver or adipose tissue of
HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice. We discussed this important point in the Discussion section.

### Reviewer 1

The authors presented a revised manuscript with more text, and new methods, data, and references. They are thanked for the extra effort. As well, the response to my comments was nicely done.
A few things came up on reading the new draft.
Several papers from the Kentucky group should be mentioned that deal with the TSP1 effect in HFD - PLoS One.
2011;6(10): e26656/ Am J Physiol Renal Physiol. 2013 Sep 15;305(6): F871-80/Sci Rep. 2023 Nov 18;13(1):20193.
The authors isolate and look at ECs from other organs and this was a nice addition. Could the implications for the paper
extend to peripheral and coronary vascular disease?
Please indicate the clone, manufacturer, concentration, etc. of the CD47 antibody used in the cell viability study. The CD47
are reported to behave as TSP1 agonists and antagonists. If the Ab worked in the cultured cells, would it work in the mice +/-
IRE1α? This would link the soluble TSP1 to the cell surface receptor/target.
Please confirm the identity of the murine islet EC line as they seem to be first described in the 1990s. These data could be
placed in a supplement.

### Reviewer 2

I appreciate the authors' efforts in addressing some of my initial concerns. However, significant scientific limitations remain,
particularly regarding the methodology and data interpretation.
1. Regarding the validation of the genetic mouse model, I appreciate the authors' additional validation efforts, including the
analysis of other tissues involved in glucose homeostasis. However, the provided evidence remains insufficient. The RNA-seq
data alone does not adequately confirm efficient gene deletion in endothelial cells within islets. Additionally, the Western
blot presented are only a representative image, with n=2, which is inadequate for proper validation. A more robust
quantification, such as qPCR or Western blot from multiple biological replicates, is necessary to strengthen the conclusions.
2. Regarding the Cre Control mice, I appreciate the authors' efforts in addressing this concern and providing additional data.
However, it would have been valuable to include insulin measurements in these control mice to fully assess the potential
effects of Cre expression. The absence of such data limits the ability to completely rule out confounding factors.
3. I remain unconvinced about the authors' conclusions regarding glucose intolerance and insulin secretion in their mouse
models. A major issue is that glucose tolerance data (Fig. 1f, Fig. 8c) is reported at week 20, whereas insulin levels are
shown separately at week 24 (Fig. 1i, Fig. 8e). The authors never present glucose and insulin data together during glucose
tolerance tests, which is inappropriate and prevents a proper interpretation of β-cell function, as I previously mentioned.
Furthermore, they report an increase in fasting insulin levels without any change in fasting glucose levels (Fig. 1h). How do
the authors explain this finding if there is no alteration in insulin sensitivity? This raises concerns about the interpretation of
their metabolic phenotyping and suggests a need for additional analyses to clarify the mechanisms at play.
4. I appreciate that the authors have now included data from female mice. However, this aspect must at least be properly
discussed in the manuscript and not only reported in the results section. Additionally, all sections of the manuscript should
be revised to clearly state that the reported findings apply only to male mice. This is essential for transparency and aligns
with Nature Communications’ guidelines on sex as a biological variable.
5. I still have major methodological Issues and concerns regarding Data Presentation:
- There are major methodological flaws in the way β-cell and α-cell areas and mass are calculated. The authors do not report
cell areas relative to total islet area, which is the correct approach. Since they claim to observe differences in islet size, this
alone could explain the observed changes in β-cell area. Similarly, β-cell mass should always be normalized to total
pancreatic mass, which was not done.
- Another inconsistency lies in the choice of methodology: in some cases, the authors report results from isolated islets rather
than pancreatic sections, without providing any justification or methodological details. This raises concerns about data
interpretation and reproducibility. Additionally, as the authors themselves acknowledge, studying endothelial cells within
islets is technically challenging. Given that the majority of endothelial cells die within a few hours of islet isolation and
culture, how can the authors reliably assess β-cell markers in isolated islets rather than in pancreatic sections? This
methodological choice is problematic and further weakens their conclusions.
- Regarding histological analyses, the authors present data for each islet analyzed within a single mouse, but with a limited
number of mice per group. This is an inappropriate method for statistical analysis, as each mouse should be considered an
independent biological replicate (n=1), rather than pooling all islets from the same mouse as individual data points. A
striking example is Fig. 4b, where the authors plot 80–100 analyzed islets per mouse in a statistical test based on only n=4
per group, which is methodologically incorrect.
- Additionally, in Fig. 3f–k, islets were pooled from three mice per group and then divided into three replicates for GSIS
analysis. Pooling islets from different mice and then artificially generating replicates significantly reduces biological
variability, making the results appear more statistically favorable. This approach is not methodologically rigorous and once
again weakens the interpretation of the findings.
- More broadly, the sample sizes (n=3–4 per group) remain too low across multiple experiments to support robust
conclusions. Increasing n and using appropriate statistical approaches are necessary to strengthen the validity of the
findings.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have performed additional experiments and provided clarifications for the concerns raised int he previous
review.
They now provide a more detailed analyses of:
1) Vascular density in the islets by performing staining with CD31 and CD34. However, CD34 might not be expressed on all
of the capillary endothelial cells. Staining with CDH5 (VEcadherin) could have been more revealing.
2) They now use human umbilical vein endothelial cells in addition to immortalized endothelial cell cell lines.
3)) They provide explanation that insulin intolerance in the IREa vascular knock out mice is not due off targeted effect of the
thrombospondin on the adipose or muscle or liver tissue.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In the present manuscript the authors test the idea that IRE1α alters the vascular network of islets to impeach their function through intersecting antiangiogenic TSP1. The hypothesis is tested using a range of approaches foremost being mutant mice that lack IRE1α in vascular endothelial cells uniformly and pathway suppression with siRNA methods. Young mice lacking IRE1α were fed a diet high in fat and metabolic readouts characterized. The text is further supported by helpful supplemental figures with control data. Overall, the composition is clear and easy to follow. A few minor usage issues were encountered but not enough to detract from the reading of the text. The data support the conclusions mostly, although certain aspects lack signaling direction and specificity and these points are explained in detail below.
Strategic/novelty: The hypothesis is new, as are the findings. However, a link between IRE1α and TSP1 was noted (J Cell Mol Med. 2022 Oct;26(20):5303-5314). Further, links between human islets and TSP1 and the dominant TSP1 receptor CD47 was published (Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab. 2023 Apr 1;324(4): E347-E357). Also, a link between TSP1-CD47 and glucose homeostasis was made in mice on a HFD (Cells. 2020 Jul 15;9(7):1695). These points are emphasized not to lessen the present work. Still these references should be covered in the Introduction and/or Discussion section of the manuscript to give a balanced presentation of the existing literature in relation to the new findings.
Balance in presentation: Not to belabor the ideas noted above, but here is an example of limited and erroneous use of citations by the authors. They cite the following 2 papers when introducing their data on TSP1 – (1) Molecular basis for the regulation of angiogenesis by thrombospondin-1 and -2. Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med 2, a006627 (2012) from Jack Lawler at Harvard. The issue here is the year of publication 2012 so it misses many more recent findings. The second citation, Thrombospondin 1 in Metabolic Diseases. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne) 12, 638536 (2021), was from folks in Pennsylvania that have done only a little work in this area. More importantly, one should always cite primary papers and in this case some that show how TSP1 limits ECs, vascular pathways, blood flow, self-renewal (see effects on cMyc), and metabolism. See Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005 Sep 13;102(37):13141-6 and others by this same group.
Methods: Please provide detailed information on animal usage: ACUC protocol #, anesthesia and euthanasia methods, balancing and mitigation of the cage effect, randomization of animals into treatment groups (was a software program used for this and if yes please state). Explain how cohort size was arrived at. Please provide details on the methods used to blind the researchers to treatment groups, etc. Justify using young mice and if only one sex was used justify why both were not studied.
Data: Counting CD31+ cells is a common metric employed to characterize vascularization. Yet, it gives no information concerning real-time tissue perfusion. This is a valid point as TSP1 seems to limit perfusion of various vascular beds separate from inhibiting cell and specifically EC proliferation and migration. Some analysis of organ (i.e., pancreas) and organoid (i.e., islet) blood flow should be made in the mice from the various treatment groups.
The paper is light on details on the signaling mechanism(s) at play. We do not the source of the TSP1 in the islets that is putatively the cause of issues and a target for IRE1α. A change in mRNA suggests a cell type may be the source but not more. The literature finds many stressed cell types from many species and people make TSP1. However, some data already pointed out in mice lacking the TSP1 signal versus circulating cell lacking TSP1 found the effect resided in the parenchyma and not in the circulating cells.
We do not know the receptors that secreated TSP1 acts through in the islets to negatively impact glucose homeostasis. One place to begin would be to look at WT and IRE1α null EC receptor patterns for primary TSP1 receptors such as CD36, CD47, beta integrins, and SIRPα. TSP1 apparently has several domains that can bind to one of these receptors and adversely alter redox pathways and metabolism. After the authors define the cell surface landscape, they should treat cells with TSP1 ± TSP1 receptor blockers and then characterize proliferation, cell death, etc.
The authors might also consider testing possible direct effects of IRE1α on vascular nitric oxide. See Mol Cells. 2018 Nov 30;41(11):964-970 and Aging (Albany NY). 2023 Dec 13;15(23):13608-13627.
Why was there had only a partial loss in IRE1α protein in the lung EC of the mutant mice. All westerns need molecular marker dye lane. I find just placing the expected MW adjacent to a blot leaves out key information that as the reader I wish to consider for myself. Included the original full blots too.
Many blots of TSP1 find it at about 150 kD. The blot in Fig. 5F has it assigned a MW of 170. Please comment on this. BTW, TSP1 is up in the plasma of people with T1 and T2 diabetes. The Discussion section should point this out and cite the several papers that showed this.
This being the case, I am wondering if more detail in plasma TSP1 analysis can be given. Care is needed to not activate platelets as they were found decades ago to hold lots of pre-made TSP1. And the lack of impact of HF diet on plasma TSP1 is curious. Would a longer disease timeline alter this?
The TSP1 translation blocking morpholino gave only a partial suppression. Was a dose and time interval study done to optimize the conditions?
Additional information: A table summarizing all antibodies, manufacture details, dilutions, and validation of specificity information should be included.
Figures: These were nicely done, and one can get the point fast. And the legends were well done with n numbers and stat test used included for each.

### Reviewer 2

The main finding of this manuscript is that genetic depletion of IRE1 alpha in endothelial cells leads to glucose intolerance, blunted intra-islet angiogenesis, compensatory islet growth and enhanced endothelial cells thbs1 expression in high-fat diet-fed mice. Further, the author report that genetic deletion of thbs1 in endothelial cells corrected the defects in glucose homeostasis observed in HFD-fed mice with genetic deletion of IRE1alpha in endothelial cells. The authors conclude that their findings “uncover a critical role of the endothelial IRE1alpha suppression of THBS1 in governing the vascular support that enables the functional adaptation of islets during metabolic stress”. However, substantial issues have been identified that limit the interpretation of the data.
Comments:
- The genetic mouse models need further validation, including confirmation that gene expression and protein levels of IRE1alpha and THBS1 are significantly reduced in other tissues than lung, especially in islets and in tissues involved in glucose homeostasis, but also confirmation that their levels are not altered in other cell types than endothelial cells.
- For the in vivo studies, the authors must show data from VE-cadherin-Cre-ERT2 mice without tamoxifen injection to confirm that data are not related to the CRE expression only.
- Based on the data shown on both Figure 1 and figure 8, the authors cannot conclude that there is glucose intolerance and deficient insulin production. Indeed, the authors report insulin data without taking in account and correcting for glucose data at the same time. The authors can absolutely not conclude that fasting insulin and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion are decreased without reporting the glucose data, since insulin is dependent on glucose levels. Further, on both figure 1 and figure 8, glucose tolerance must be calculated as iAUC during the OGTT.
- The authors must report data in female and/or at least justify why they did only report data in male mice
- Information about the methods and experiments is lacking throughout the manuscript. For example, there is no information regarding how blood was drawn for insulin measurement (Fig 1) or how islets were processed for insulin content measurement (Fig 2). For histo and immunohistochemistry, the authors must have used IgG isotype as negative controls for staining. The n are very low for several experiments; only representative images of one experiment are shown (e.g. Fig 1b, Fig S1,..) and some figures show only replicate of one experiment (e.g. GSIS and perifusion data on Fig3).
- Beta-cell and alpha cell area and mass rather than % of alpha and beta-cell must be correctly calculated and reported to allow the authors to conclude there are changes in islet morphology.

### Reviewer 3

In this report, the authors demonstrate that genetic deletion of the inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1α) specifically in the endothelial cells of the adult mice, results in the poor response of the vascular cells to the metabolic stress induced by enforced obesity secondary to chronic high fat diet (HFD) intake. These abnormalities in IRE1α deficient endothelial cells were manifested in subtle glucose intolerance with impaired insulin secretion. The mechanism of this metabolic dysregulation was mediated through upregulation of the mRNA encoding presumed anti-angiogenic agent thrombospondin-1 (THBS1/TSP1). IRE1α RNase15 mediated mRNA decay of THBS1 presumably modulate the overall expression of this factor in SV40 large T antigen immortalized MS1 mouse endothelial cells. Knock down of THBS1 in endothelial cells restored the islet vascular defects arising from endothelial cell-IRE1α deficiency in response to HDF induced obesity.
Comments:
The mechanism by which neo-angiogenesis might play a role in the regulation of obesity induced metabolic dysfunction is not known. Demonstration that IRE1α deficiency through upregulation of THBS1 might interfere with angiogenic activity in the islets thereby contributing to metabolic derangements afforded by chronic HDF induced obesity could have therapeutic implications.
However, the data presented are not that convincing and many of the conclusions are not strongly supported by the data provided.
1) The majority of the changes in glucose levels and insulin intolerance in the IRE1α deficient mice are only marginal, which are corrected with the THBS1 knock down. Indeed, the pathophysiological consequences of those metabolic changes are not readily apparent. Are there any pathological changes in the cardiovascular function, liver metabolism or kidney function in the IRE1α deficient mice ?
2) It is unclear whether the subtle differences in hyperglycemia and insulin intolerance are primarily due to pancreatic dysfunction or increase in the adipose tissue vascular mass changes secondary to the chronic HFD induced obesity? Is there a correlation with the increase vascular mass index with the metabolic changes potentially in the adipose tissue of the IRE1α or THBS1 deficient mice.
3) The authors claim that there could be a defect in the islet angiogenesis in the IRE1α or THBS1 deficient mice. However, whether there are changes in the vessel density and as to how these changes lead to metabolic abnormalities observed is not well characterized. In figure 4 the authors use CD31 (PECAM) as the marker for endothelial cell staining. However, CD31 staining is not sufficient to specifically stain endothelial cells as CD31 is also expressed on hematopoietic cells including inflammatory monocytes and macrophages. Other vascular specific markers such as VE-cadherin or CD34 might be considered.
4) The use of mouse MS1 SV40 large T antigen immortalized endothelial cells could be fraught with artifacts because metabolically these cells employ oxidative phosphorylation, but not glycolysis, secondary to oncogenic transformation possibly obscuring the effects I IRE1α and XBP1 mediated stress responses. Use of more primary isolated endothelial cells, preferably from the metabolic organs might be more revealing.
5) In IRE1α deficient mice there are also changes in the expression and RNA decay of other factors. Then, is THBS1 dysregulation the main factor that contributes to the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction in the IRE1α mice? Why the authors elected to focus on THBS1 and not the other factors.
6) THBS1 has many different pleiotropic effects on regulating blood vessel integrity. Besides potential anti-angiogenic effect, THSP1 could also modulate homeostatic functions of blood vessels not only in the pancreas but also in adipose or liver vasculature. Then, to what extent the metabolic changes in IRE1α or THSP1 deficient mice, could be attributed to its anti-angiogenic activity?

the various treatment groups.
Response:
We followed the suggestions from the Reviewer and measured the blood perfusion in
pancreas and white adipose tissue of NC- and HFD-fed mice using MoorFLPI-2 blood
flow imager. We did not observe apparent changes of blood flow in these tissues
examined (data were presented in Supplemental Fig. S7), suggesting that endothelial
IRE1α ablation likely had no obvious impact upon the blood flow rate. So far, we have
not been able to find reliable methodology that can be readily utilized to precisely
measure the blood flow within the islets, and we wish not to speculate too much on this
point.
4) The paper is light on details on the signaling mechanism(s) at play. We do not the
source of the TSP1 in the islets that is putatively the cause of issues and a target for
IRE1α. A change in mRNA suggests a cell type may be the source but not more. The
literature finds many stressed cell types from many species and people make TSP1.
However, some data already pointed out in mice lacking the TSP1 signal versus
circulating cell lacking TSP1 found the effect resided in the parenchyma and not in the
circulating cells. We do not know the receptors that secreted TSP1 acts through in the
islets to negatively impact glucose homeostasis. One place to begin would be to look at
WT and IRE1α null EC receptor patterns for primary TSP1 receptors such as CD36,
CD47, beta integrins, and SIRPα. TSP1 apparently has several domains that can bind
to one of these receptors and adversely alter redox pathways and metabolism. After the
authors define the cell surface landscape, they should treat cells with TSP1 ± TSP1
receptor blockers and then characterize proliferation, cell death, etc.
The authors might also consider testing possible direct effects of IRE1α on vascular
nitric oxide. See Mol Cells. 2018 Nov 30;41(11):964-970 and Aging (Albany NY).
Response:
Following the suggestions from the Reviewer, we further explored the signaling
mechanisms at play. Based on the scRNA-seq analysis of islets (data were presented in
Supplemental Fig. S11), we focused on the TSP1-CD47 axis in ECs and examined the
effect of blocking CD47 with a neutralizing antibody in MS1 cells upon cell
proliferation (data were presented in Fig. 6j). In addition, we also examined the impact
of IRE1α ablation upon islet eNOS as well as that of TSP1 upon eNOS in MS1 cells
(data were presented in Supplemental Fig. S12). While we could not detect changes in
eNOS in TSP1-treated MS1 cells, we detected decreased eNOS expression in islets with
IRE1α deficiency in ECs. This again supports the multi-tasked nature of IRE1α function,
and as a matter of fact, we have been studying, as an independent research project,
this
interesting point in more detail with respect to its mechanistic function in blood pressure
control.
5) Why was there had only a partial loss in IRE1α protein in the lung EC of the mutant
mice. All westerns need molecular marker dye lane. I find just placing the expected
MW adjacent to a blot leaves out key information that as the reader I wish to consider
for myself. Included the original full blots too. Many blots of TSP1 find it at about 150
kD. The blot in Fig. 5F has it assigned a MW of 170. Please comment on this. BTW,
TSP1 is up in the plasma of people with T1 and T2 diabetes. The Discussion section
should point this out and cite the several papers that showed this. This being the case, I
am wondering if more detail in plasma TSP1 analysis can be given. Care is needed to
not activate platelets as they were found decades ago to hold lots of pre-made TSP1.
And the lack of impact of HF diet on plasma TSP1 is curious. Would a longer disease
timeline alter this?
Response:
Usually the EC fraction from the lung would contain cells of other types due to non-
specific binding to the beads used, from which IRE1α protein can still be detected by
Western immunoblot analysis. To confirm the efficiency of IRE1α depletion, we
optimized the isolation procedure and analyzed ECs isolated from the liver, lung and
heart, and our results more clearly showed efficient ablation of IRE1α in Ern1EC-KO ECs
(data were presented in Fig. 1c). Due to the limited space for figures containing all the
immunoblots, we chose to show one MW marker near the protein of interest without
including the MW marker dye lane. We will provide all the original full blots in the
Supplemental Materials and the Reporting Summary as requested by the journal if
accepted for publication. The immunoblot of TSP1 in the previous Fig. 5F showed a
MW position below 170, which appeared closer to 170 because of shorter running time
of the PAGE. For the association of TSP1 with human diabetes, we added a recent
review (PMID: 34106789) on the topic in Discussion to avoid citing too many reference
papers. For the impact of HFD feeding upon circulating TSP1, our data also showed
increased serum TSP1 levels in the obese group (presented in Supplemental Fig S9),
which is in line with reported results. We used the standard protocol for serum TSP1
protein measurement as described in the Methods section. While it is not easy to assess
whether platelets may have produced a major proportion of circulating TSP1,
apparently no significant contributions could be seen from EC-derived TSP1 protein in
the context of endothelial IRE1α depletion.
6) The TSP1 translation blocking morpholino gave only a partial suppression. Was a
dose and time interval study done to optimize the conditions? Additional information:
A table summarizing all antibodies, manufacture details, dilutions, and validation of
specificity information should be included.
Response: We actually utilized lentiviral shRNA to knock down the expression of TSP1
in MS1 cells (Fig 6h). Usually a 36-48-hour infection would do for the knockdown
experiment, and an incomplete suppression of the target gene is not surprising. We
followed the Reviewer’s suggestions and included a summary table for all the desired
information (Supplemental Table S4).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The main finding of this manuscript is that genetic depletion of IRE1 alpha in
endothelial cells leads to glucose intolerance, blunted intra-islet angiogenesis,
compensatory islet growth and enhanced endothelial cells thbs1 expression in high-fat
diet-fed mice. Further, the author report that genetic deletion of thbs1 in endothelial
cells corrected the defects in glucose homeostasis observed in HFD-fed mice with
genetic deletion of IRE1alpha in endothelial cells. The authors conclude that their
findings “uncover a critical role of the endothelial IRE1alpha suppression of THBS1 in
governing the vascular support that enables the functional adaptation of islets during
metabolic stress”. However, substantial issues have been identified that limit the
interpretation of the data.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the Reviewer’s constructive and critical comments.
Comments
1) The genetic mouse models need further validation, including confirmation that gene
expression and protein levels of IRE1alpha and THBS1 are significantly reduced in
other tissues than lung, especially in islets and in tissues involved in glucose
homeostasis, but also confirmation that their levels are not altered in other cell types
than endothelial cells.
Response:
We followed the suggestions from the Reviewer and further validated the genetic
mouse model. We analyzed additional tissues involved in glucose homeostasis,
including the liver and heart. We confirmed the efficient depletion of IRE1α and
THBS1 in CD31+ endothelial cells in Ern1EC-KO and Ern1EC-KO;Thbs1EC-KO mice,
using CD31- cells as the negative control. These data were presented in Fig.1c and
Supplemental Fig. S14a. Owing to the technical difficulty in isolating islet ECs,
which is generally known to the relevant research field, we analyzed the RNA-seq
data and confirmed the efficient deletion of the exon 2 of Ern1 gene in Ern1EC-KO
mice (Supplemental Fig. S8a).
2) For the in vivo studies, the authors must show data from VE-cadherin-Cre-ERT2
mice without tamoxifen injection to confirm that data are not related to the CRE
expression only.
Following the suggestions from the Reviewer, we performed metabolic phenotyping
analyses of Ern1fl/fl and Ern1fl/fl;VE-cad-CreERT2 mice without tamoxifen treatment
following HFD feeding for 12 weeks. We confirmed that the observed changes in islet
adaptation of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice are not related to the Cre expression only. These
data were presented in Supplemental Fig. S4.
3) Based on the data shown on both Figure 1 and figure 8, the authors cannot conclude
that there is glucose intolerance and deficient insulin production. Indeed, the authors
report insulin data without taking in account and correcting for glucose data at the same
time. The authors can absolutely not conclude that fasting insulin and glucose-
stimulated insulin secretion are decreased without reporting the glucose data, since
insulin is dependent on glucose levels. Further, on both figure 1 and figure 8, glucose
tolerance must be calculated as iAUC during the OGTT.
Response:
We totally understand the Reviewer’s concerns and presented the metabolic data more
clearly. We included the iAUC for the GTT results in both Fig 1f and Fig 8c, which
showed significant impairment of glucose tolerance in HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO but not in
HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO;Thbs1EC-KO mice relative to their control littermates. We also
included the data on serum glucose levels of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice after a 4-hour
fast when showing their serum insulin levels (Fig. 1h), which suggests the reduced
insulin levels did not result from lower glucose levels. For glucose-stimulated insulin
secretion in vivo, we observed marked reductions in insulin levels from HFD-fed
Ern1EC-KO mice (Fig. 1i) following glucose stimulation during the GTT (Fig. 1f),
indicating significantly impaired insulin production even in the face of higher blood
glucose levels in HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice.
4) The authors must report data in female and/or at least justify why they did only report
data in male mice.
Response:
We followed the suggestions from the Reviewer and performed dietary obesity analysis
for female Ern1EC-KO and Ern1fl/fl mice, which showed lower sensitivity to HFD-
induced obesity (data were presented in Supplemental Fig. S3 of the revised
manuscript). This is in accordance with results from previously documented studies (e.g.
PMID: 33308894). This is why male mice are usually used in the field for metabolic
studies of dietary obesity.
5) Information about the methods and experiments is lacking throughout the manuscript.
For example, there is no information regarding how blood was drawn for insulin
measurement (Fig 1) or how islets were processed for insulin content measurement (Fig
2). For histo and immunohistochemistry, the authors must have used IgG isotype as
negative controls for staining. The n are very low for several experiments; only
representative images of one experiment are shown (e.g. Fig 1b, Fig S1,..) and some
figures show only replicate of one experiment (e.g. GSIS and perifusion data on Fig3).
Response:
We appreciate these important points from the Reviewer and included the information
about the methods and experiments in the Methods section, including how blood was
drawn for insulin measurement and how islets were processed for insulin content
measurement. For immunohistochemistry staining analysis of Insulin, CD31 and CD34
from pancreas sections, we used IgG as the negative control (Supplemental Fig. S6a).
For key metabolic phenotypes, we combined the n from repeated independent cohorts
for reaching a higher n number. Usually we presented representative images from at
least two independent experiments. We removed the flow-cytometry data in Fig 1b of
the previous manuscript as we employed a better method for isolating tissue ECs as
described in the Methods section. For islet perifusion data, we showed results from
pooled islets of HFD-fed mice (n=3 mice for each group, 2 independent animal cohorts).
For islet GSIS assay, we presented data from pooled islets in one animal cohort study
(Fig 3f), and similar data from another independent study, which is difficult to combine
when presenting the actual insulin valuse, is shown below for your information.
Primary islets of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice showed decreased glucose stimulated
insulin secretion.
6) Beta-cell and alpha cell area and mass rather than % of alpha and beta-cell must be
correctly calculated and reported to allow the authors to conclude there are changes in
islet morphology.
Response:
Following the Reviewer’s suggestions, we calculated β cell and α cell areas in islets of
the pancreas sections (presented in Fig. 3b and Fig. 3c), in addition to their proportions
in islets of Ern1EC-KO mice after HFD feeding. We also determined β cell mass in
primary islets from these models in Fig 4e.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this report, the authors demonstrate that genetic deletion of the inositol-requiring
enzyme 1 (IRE1α) specifically in the endothelial cells of the adult mice, results in the
poor response of the vascular cells to the metabolic stress induced by enforced obesity
secondary to chronic high fat diet (HFD) intake. These abnormalities in IRE1α deficient
endothelial cells were manifested in subtle glucose intolerance with impaired insulin
secretion. The mechanism of this metabolic dysregulation was mediated through
upregulation of the mRNA encoding presumed anti-angiogenic agent thrombospondin-
1 (THBS1/TSP1). IRE1α RNase15 mediated mRNA decay of THBS1 presumably
modulate the overall expression of this factor in SV40 large T antigen immortalized
MS1 mouse endothelial cells. Knock down of THBS1 in endothelial cells restored the
islet vascular defects arising from endothelial cell-IRE1α deficiency in response to HDF
induced obesity.
Comments:
The mechanism by which neo-angiogenesis might play a role in the regulation of
obesity induced metabolic dysfunction is not known. Demonstration that IRE1α
deficiency through upregulation of THBS1 might interfere with angiogenic activity in
the islets thereby contributing to metabolic derangements afforded by chronic HDF
induced obesity could have therapeutic implications.
However, the data presented are not that convincing and many of the conclusions are
not strongly supported by the data provided.
Response:
We really appreciate the Reviewer’s constructive and critical comments.
1) The majority of the changes in glucose levels and insulin intolerance in the IRE1α
deficient mice are only marginal, which are corrected with the THBS1 knock down.
Indeed, the pathophysiological consequences of those metabolic changes are not readily
apparent. Are there any pathological changes in the cardiovascular function, liver
metabolism or kidney function in the IRE1α deficient mice ?
Response:
We do agree with Reviewer in that endothelial IRE1α depletion did not lead to very
dramatic changes in glucose metabolism and insulin intolerance, but it did result in
impaired islet adaptation following HFD feeding. While we are very interested in
conducting more thorough studies such as the effects on their cardiovascular function,
liver metabolism and kidney function in this animal model, we did not observe apparent
pathological changes in their heart or kidney function. Surely enough, we will look into
opportunities for collaborating with colleagues in relevant fields to investigate these
important questions using appropriate stress conditions in the future. In the current
dietary obesity model, we conducted more experiments to examine lipid metabolism in
the liver, and we observed elevated levels of hepatic TAG and cholesterol in HFD-fed
Ern1EC-KO mice (data presented in Supplemental Fig. S1g and S1h), despite no apparent
histological changes in the liver via H/E staining analysis. Because this study focused
on glucose metabolism under obesity-induced metabolic stress, we would like to further
investigate in more mechanistic detail the role of endothelial IRE1α in hepatic lipid
metabolism following NASH-diet feeding or liver injuries. In this case, we will actively
seek more sufficient research funding support for these highly interesting studies in the
future.
2) It is unclear whether the subtle differences in hyperglycemia and insulin intolerance
are primarily due to pancreatic dysfunction or increase in the adipose tissue vascular
mass changes secondary to the chronic HFD induced obesity? Is there a correlation with
the increase vascular mass index with the metabolic changes potentially in the adipose
tissue of the IRE1α or THBS1 deficient mice.
Response:
This is a very insightful point that, in fact, led us to establish initially the DIO model,
as we anticipated a likely impact of endothelial IRE1α depletion upon adipose tissue
function in obesity. Unexpectedly but intriguingly, we found that the intra-islet ECs are
most sensitive to the loss of IRE1α during dietary obesity. We did not observe
significant alterations in the vascular density in adipose tissue of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO
mice (Supplemental Fig. S6e-g) or HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO;Thbs1EC-KO mice (Supplemental
Fig. S14b). This may reflect the distinct regulatory actions of endothelial IRE1α in
different tissues.
3) The authors claim that there could be a defect in the islet angiogenesis in the IRE1α
or THBS1 deficient mice. However, whether there are changes in the vessel density and
as to how these changes lead to metabolic abnormalities observed is not well
characterized. In figure 4 the authors use CD31 (PECAM) as the marker for endothelial
cell staining. However, CD31 staining is not sufficient to specifically stain endothelial
cells as CD31 is also expressed on hematopoietic cells including inflammatory
monocytes and macrophages. Other vascular specific markers such as VE-cadherin or
CD34 might be considered.
Response:
Following the Reviewer’s suggestions, we more carefully characterized the vascular
density in pancreatic islets, liver and adipose tissue of NC- and HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO
mice using CD31 as well as CD34 as the EC staining marker (Supplemental Fig. S6).
Consistently, we detected significantly reduced abundance of intra-islet ECs but not in
the liver or adipose tissue of HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice, suggesting defective angiogenic
capacity in the islets under metabolic stress.
4) The use of mouse MS1 SV40 large T antigen immortalized endothelial cells could
be fraught with artifacts because metabolically these cells employ oxidative
phosphorylation, but not glycolysis, secondary to oncogenic transformation possibly
obscuring the effects I IRE1α and XBP1 mediated stress responses. Use of more
primary isolated endothelial cells, preferably from the metabolic organs might be more
revealing.
Response:
We appreciate this important point from the Reviewer. We followed the suggestions
and used primary HUVECs for dissecting the effect of IRE1α knockdown upon TSP1
expression (Supplemental Fig 6b, 6d and 6f). Notably, similar results were obtained as
in MS1 cells.
5) In IRE1α deficient mice there are also changes in the expression and RNA decay of
other factors. Then, is THBS1 dysregulation the main factor that contributes to the
pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction in the IRE1α mice? Why the authors elected to
focus on THBS1 and not the other factors.
Response:
We identified THBS1 as one of the top-ranked downregulated target genes as a result
of IRE1α ablation (Fig. 5). Moreover, based on the scRNA-seq analysis of HFD-fed
islets (accession No. GSE203376), we found that its expression is specifically restricted
to ECs along with the EC marker Cdh5 (Fig S10). Given TSP1 as a well-established
endogenous antiangiogenic factor that not only inhibits EC proliferation but also exerts
multiple regulatory effects upon glucose and lipid metabolism through affecting the
adipose tissue as well as pancreatic islets, we chose to focus on this molecule as a
potential downstream effector of IRE1α. Indeed, depletion of TSP1 in the context of
IRE1α ablation completely corrected the metabolic defects during dietary obesity (Fig
8), supporting that THBS1 dysregulation is the main factor contributing to the
metabolic dysfunction of islets in EC-specific IRE1α-deficient mice during dietary
obesity.
6) THBS1 has many different pleiotropic effects on regulating blood vessel integrity.
Besides potential anti-angiogenic effect, THSP1 could also modulate homeostatic
functions of blood vessels not only in the pancreas but also in adipose or liver
vasculature. Then, to what extent the metabolic changes in IRE1α or THSP1 deficient
mice, could be attributed to its anti-angiogenic activity?
Response:
We agree with the Reviewer in that IRE1α or TSP1 in ECs may exert additional
regulatory effects upon the endocrine cells in the islets, e.g. through intercellular
interactions that remain to be elucidated, in addition to their anti-angiogenic activity.
Nonetheless, our results together from the animal models and cell-based assays indicate
that the effect of TSP1’s anti-angiogenic activity in islets most likely serves as one
major contributor to the metabolic changes arising from endothelial IRE1α deficiency,
as we observed no overt changes in vascular density in the liver or adipose tissue of
HFD-fed Ern1EC-KO mice. We discussed this important point in the Discussion section.
